languages.name: COBOL
languages.shortDescription: Business-oriented programming language, widely used in banking, financial, and public-sector systems.
languages.longDescription:
The name COBOL comes from Common Business-Oriented Language.
It is a HIGH-LEVEL language designed for data processing, with excellent portability across different systems. In other words, it resembles human language, using programming words, verbs, and expressions that are similar to English.
It is a STRUCTURED language. It provides a programming approach that enables the development of reliable and efficient programs while also making the source code easier to understand. This not only provides advantages during the development phase but also makes subsequent modifications and maintenance easier.
It does not support scientific or trigonometric calculations, but it does support the decimal arithmetic functions commonly used in business processing, which makes it easier to understand and use for business applications.
It provides facilities for processing character strings and character data.
Created in 1959 with the support of the DoD (United States Department of Defense), COBOL was the first programming language specifically designed for business applications. At the time, every system that was purchased or outsourced could be written in a different language, often machine-dependent assembly languages such as NCR NEAT/3, resulting in significant costs for maintaining these heterogeneous systems.
It was developed by the Conference on Data Systems Languages (CODASYL). This committee was the result of a joint effort involving industry, leading universities, and the United States Government.
Grace Hopper played a key role in its development. While working for the United States Navy, she had designed FLOW-MATIC, a language that strongly influenced COBOL.
languages.examples:
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION. 
PROGRAM-ID. PRG01.
ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.
CONFIGURATION SECTION.
SOURCE-COMPUTER. IBM-370.
OBJECT-COMPUTER. IBM-370.
INPUT-OUTPUT SECTION.
FILE-CONTROL. 
  SELECT ENTRADA
  ASSIGN TO ENTRADA
DATA DIVISION.
FILE SECTION.
FD ENTRADA
   LABEL RECORDS ARE OMITTED.
01 INFILE-REC PIC X (80).
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
 01 VARIABLE PIC X (100).
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
  DISPLAY 'HELLO WORLD'.

languages.name: JCL
languages.shortDescription: Job Control Language used to execute programs, define datasets, and control batch processes in z/OS.
languages.longDescription:
JCL is the language used to execute programs and utilities in batch mode.
Batch processing for job input and output in the operating system is controlled by an operating-system subsystem called JES. There are two versions: JES2 and JES3.
JES reads input through the READER component and handles output through the WRITER component, which can route output to printers and other destinations.
The main function of JES is to prepare jobs for execution by interpreting the control statements that make up each JOB and allocating the resources required for execution, including the address space in which the job will run.
These jobs are written in a specialized job control language called JOB CONTROL LANGUAGE, or JCL for short.
JES is invoked whenever a JCL job is submitted using the TSO primary command: SUB job-name.
At this point, a file containing the control statements to be executed is placed in the job input queue. JES then assigns a job identification number and creates a SYSOUT data set containing the results of the job execution.
JCL control statements primarily specify the programs to be executed, as well as the input files or datasets they will access and the output files or datasets they will create. The required resources for these datasets are also specified so that they can be allocated during execution.

languages.name: CICS
languages.shortDescription: Transaction monitor used for high-performance online applications in mainframe environments.
languages.longDescription:
CICS, an acronym for Customer Information Control System, is a transaction manager, or teleprocessing monitor, developed by IBM. It is a key component of online transaction processing (OLTP) systems and runs primarily on IBM mainframes with operating systems such as z/OS and z/VSE.
CICS versions have also existed for other environments, such as OS/400 and OS/2. There is also a version for Unix environments, known as TXSeries.
It is a general-purpose data management system capable of operating across networks with a large number of terminals, potentially thousands of them.
Today, it is one of the most widely deployed transaction processing systems in the world.
Transaction Management: CICS manages online and batch transactions, allowing thousands of transactions per second to be processed on mainframe systems.
Multilanguage Support: CICS applications can be written in several programming languages, including COBOL, PL/I, C, C++, Assembler, REXX, and Java.
Resource Interaction: CICS provides services for interacting with files, databases, terminals, and web services.
Transaction Recovery: CICS manages transactions so that, if part of a transaction fails, all recoverable changes can be backed out.
Middleware: CICS acts as middleware, providing services that can be more efficient than general-purpose operating-system services.
languages.examples:
EXEC CICS SEND MAP('MENU') MAPSET('MENUS') END-EXEC
EXEC CICS RECEIVE MAP('MENU') INTO(WS-MENU) END-EXEC

languages.name: DB2
languages.shortDescription: Relational database management system used in batch and online applications.
languages.longDescription:
IBM Db2, one of the best-known database management systems, has a fascinating history dating back to the 1960s and 1970s, when storing large amounts of data on mainframes such as the System/360 was becoming increasingly challenging due to cost and complexity.
Mathematician Edgar F. Codd, while working at the IBM San Jose Research Laboratory, published a groundbreaking paper in 1970 proposing a new approach to database management: the relational model, which will be covered later.
Despite IBM's initial resistance, as the company was still promoting its hierarchical database system, IBM IMS, the potential of the relational model was undeniable.
In 1973, IBM launched the System R project at its San Jose laboratory with the goal of creating a robust implementation of the relational model. Although Codd did not participate directly in the project, his theory formed the foundation on which it was developed.
Finally, in 1983, IBM released Db2, adopting the relational model for its MVS (Multiple Virtual Storage) operating system and marking the beginning of a new era in database management.
Although Db2 uses VSAM files to store some components, such as tablespaces, VSAM (Virtual Storage Access Method) files were not the foundation of Db2, although they did play an important role in its implementation.
VSAM files are a data access method developed by IBM to improve file performance and management on mainframe systems, which will be covered later.
Since its release, Db2 has continuously evolved, adapting to new technologies and market requirements. It is now a hybrid and multicloud platform supporting real-time analytics and high-speed transactions.
Db2 remains a cornerstone of data management, demonstrating IBM's vision and innovation in this field. From its early beginnings to its current state, Db2 has come a long way, establishing itself as an essential technology for efficient and secure data management while supporting thousands of customers and millions of users.
languages.examples:
EXEC SQL
   SELECT NOMBRE INTO :WS-NOMBRE
   FROM CLIENTES
   WHERE ID = :WS-ID
END-EXEC

languages.name: REXX
languages.shortDescription: Scripting language used for automation, utilities, and tools in TSO/ISPF.
languages.longDescription:
REXX is a programming and scripting language developed by IBM to provide a simple, powerful, and easy-to-maintain tool for task automation and application development. It was designed so that both experienced programmers and users with basic technical knowledge could quickly create programs using clear and readable syntax.
Its primary area of use has been the IBM ecosystem, particularly mainframe environments such as z/OS, TSO/E, ISPF, and VM/CMS, where it has become one of the standard languages for automating operational processes, system administration, and interaction with enterprise applications.
One of the characteristics that has contributed to its longevity is its excellent support for text-string processing, file management, and operating-system command execution. As a result, REXX has been widely used to develop operational procedures, automate repetitive tasks, manage batch jobs, and simplify day-to-day system administration.
Although many organizations now use more modern languages such as Python, Java, or PowerShell for new initiatives, REXX continues to play an important role in many enterprise environments running IBM Mainframe platforms. Sectors such as banking, insurance, telecommunications, and government continue to use it because of the stability of existing systems and the large number of critical processes developed in this language.
In summary, REXX is a scripting language focused on automation and system administration, widely deployed in the IBM mainframe world and recognized for its simplicity, maintainability, and effectiveness in managing enterprise processes.

languages.name: CLIST
languages.shortDescription: Command language used in TSO/ISPF before REXX. Still present in legacy systems.
languages.longDescription:
CLIST (Command List) is a procedural language developed by IBM to automate tasks and facilitate interaction with mainframe operating systems, particularly within the TSO/E (Time Sharing Option/Extensions) environment. It was one of the first tools used to create scripts and procedures capable of executing sequences of commands automatically, simplifying users' operational and administrative tasks.
Its primary purpose is to act as a control language that allows commands to be chained together, parameters to be managed, basic logic operations to be performed, and repetitive processes to be automated. As a result, it was widely used for many years to develop menus, interactive procedures, support utilities, and administration tools in IBM environments.
CLIST is characterized by relatively simple syntax, although it is less structured and more limited than later languages. Its ability to manage variables, control execution flow, and interact with the TSO environment allowed administrators and developers to create quick solutions for day-to-day operational requirements.
With the introduction of REXX, IBM provided a more powerful, flexible, and maintainable alternative. As a result, many new developments progressively migrated to REXX, which offered better programming capabilities, data handling, and code readability. However, CLIST remains present in many organizations because historical procedures continue to operate and form part of critical business processes.
Today, although its use is much lower than in previous decades, CLIST can still be found in traditional mainframe environments where legacy applications and procedures are maintained. Knowledge of CLIST remains particularly useful for professionals involved in the administration and maintenance of long-established IBM systems.
languages.examples:
PROC 0
WRITE Hello from CLIST
ALLOC F(TEST) DA('USER.DATA') SHR
FREE F(TEST)

languages.name: PL/I
languages.shortDescription: Programming language used in scientific, financial, and systems applications.
languages.longDescription:
In the 1950s, commercial users employed COBOL and Fortran, while scientists used Fortran and Algol. With the announcement of the IBM System/360 in 1964, IBM sought to unify both worlds in a single language.
In October 1963, a joint committee was formed consisting of three IBM engineers in New York and three members of SHARE, IBM's scientific user group, to define the extensions required by both commercial and scientific programmers.
The project began under the name NPL (New Programming Language), changed to MPPL (Multipurpose Programming Language), and in 1965 was definitively established as PL/I (Programming Language One).
The first formal specification appeared in April 1964, at which point IBM had completed the design sufficiently to write the first compiler.
The first formal PL/I specification appeared in April 1964, although the original NPL definition lacked sufficient detail to write a compiler. IBM completed the design at the New York Programming Center and later at the Hursley Laboratory in the United Kingdom, resulting in the first compiler being written in PL/I itself, an important milestone in the language's early maturity. The SHARE and GUIDE user groups participated in extending and governing the language, helping ensure that it evolved according to real production requirements.
PL/I incorporated advanced features from its beginnings, including multiprocessing, recursion, modern control structures, dynamic memory management, and debugging facilities.
It was one of the first commercial languages whose compiler was self-hosted.
IBM initially implemented it for the System/360 delivered in 1966, demonstrating the language's maturity by allowing it to compile itself and providing integrated debugging tools very early in its lifecycle.
IBM registered the PL/I trademark to control its evolution, which limited adoption by third parties, but within the IBM ecosystem it became a key technology for projects such as the Multics operating system and mission-critical mainframe applications.
1966: Delivery of the first version of the PL/I compiler for IBM System/360, enabling PL/I programs to run on OS/360 and DOS/360 platforms.
June 1, 1969: Coding of Version 1 of the PL/I compiler for the Multics operating system was completed; the bootstrap process was completed between June and October 1969, with more than 300 pages of code dedicated to the optimizer.
In 1976, ANSI published the ANSI X3.74-1976 standard, followed by revisions in 1987 and 1998 (ANSI X3.74-1987 R1998), consolidating a general-purpose subset. During the 1980s and 1990s, PL/I added extensions for multiprocessing, dynamic memory allocation, and 31/64-bit support. Today, it remains in use in IBM z/OS environments through implementations such as IBM PL/I for z/OS, coexisting with modern technologies and supporting the maintenance and modernization of mission-critical applications.

languages.name: ASSEMBLER
languages.shortDescription: Low-level assembly language used for critical routines and system utilities.
languages.longDescription:
Assembler (HLASM) is a low-level programming language that allows programs to be developed using instructions that are very close to the machine language executed directly by the processor. Unlike high-level languages, Assembler provides detailed control over hardware resources, allowing performance, memory usage, and the execution of critical processes to be optimized.
In IBM Mainframe environments, Assembler has historically played a fundamental role in the development of system components, infrastructure utilities, and applications that require a high level of efficiency. Many basic operating-system functions, as well as numerous enterprise software products, have been developed entirely or partially using this language.
Assembler works by using instructions specific to the processor architecture, represented through mnemonic codes that make source code easier to read and maintain. An assembler program subsequently translates these instructions into machine language for execution by the hardware.
Its main advantages include high performance, direct access to system resources, the ability to optimize critical processes, and precise control over memory and devices. These characteristics make it particularly suitable for system software, drivers, high-performance routines, and infrastructure components.
However, Assembler also involves greater development and maintenance complexity compared with modern languages. Programs generally require more lines of code to implement equivalent functionality and require in-depth knowledge of the underlying hardware architecture and operating system.
Despite the evolution of programming languages and the emergence of more advanced technologies, Assembler continues to be used in IBM Mainframe environments for maintaining legacy applications, developing system components, and implementing processes that require maximum performance and operational efficiency.
languages.examples:
PRINT NOGEN
MYPROG   CSECT
         STM   14,12,12(13)
         WTO   'HELLO FROM ASSEMBLER'
         BR    14

languages.name: IMS
languages.shortDescription: Hierarchical database management system and transaction monitor.
languages.longDescription:
IMS (Information Management System) is a database management and transaction processing system developed by IBM. It was designed to manage large volumes of information and support critical business applications requiring high levels of availability, performance, and reliability. Since its introduction, IMS has become one of the fundamental components of many IBM Mainframe environments.
IMS combines two main capabilities: hierarchical database management and online transaction processing. This architecture enables enterprise applications to access large amounts of data quickly and securely while maintaining data integrity and operational continuity.
As a database management system, IMS organizes information using a hierarchical structure composed of related segments. This model is particularly efficient for applications with well-defined data relationships and high-speed access requirements. As a transaction monitor, IMS manages thousands of concurrent transactions, coordinating communication between users, applications, and databases securely and efficiently.
IMS has been widely adopted in sectors where stability and large-scale processing are essential, such as banking, insurance, telecommunications, transportation, and government. Many of the most critical enterprise applications in these organizations continue to run on IMS because of its ability to operate continuously for long periods and handle high workloads.
Despite the emergence of newer technologies and relational databases, IMS continues to evolve and maintain a significant presence in large enterprises. IBM continues to introduce enhancements that facilitate its integration with modern architectures, web services, APIs, and distributed environments, allowing applications developed on IMS to remain part of modern technology strategies.
languages.examples:
CALL 'CBLTDLI' USING GU, PCB, SEGMENT-AREA;
IF STATUS-CODE = ' ' THEN PROCESS-SEGMENT;

languages.name: DFSORT / ICETOOL
languages.shortDescription: Utility for sorting, filtering, and transforming datasets in batch processes.
languages.longDescription:
SORT, or DFSORT, is one of the products in the IBM Data Facility family integrated into z/OS. It is a high-performance data processing utility developed by IBM to sort, merge, filter, and transform large volumes of data.
DFSORT is a mainframe-specific utility used to process and manipulate sequential files with the help of JCL and other mainframe utilities that can run in the background.
It uses split-merge algorithms optimized for memory and disk, providing high performance on mainframe systems.
It includes extensions such as ICETOOL for report generation, record counting, and advanced operations without requiring additional processing steps.
It allows operations to be performed on files such as sorting, merging records, removing duplicate records, extracting records according to specific conditions, reformatting records, and merging data with other files.
DFSORT originated in the 1970s as an evolution of IBM's original SORT command for MVS systems, changing its name to reflect its integration with other system utilities.
It became part of the Data Facility family with the goal of providing mainframe administrators with a specialized tool for sequential-file processing.
Throughout the 1980s, it became a standard technology in enterprise environments that needed to sort and manipulate millions of records every day.

languages.name: RACF
languages.shortDescription: Access control and security facility in z/OS.
languages.longDescription:
RACF (Resource Access Control Facility) is IBM's security solution for controlling and protecting access to resources in z/OS Mainframe environments. Its primary objective is to ensure that only authorized users, applications, and processes can access system information and resources, thereby contributing to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of corporate data.
RACF is one of the fundamental components of the security architecture of IBM Mainframe systems. It acts as a centralized authentication, authorization, and auditing system, managing user identities and defining which actions they can perform on different resources. These resources include datasets, applications, transactions, queues, printers, system commands, and other critical infrastructure components.
Security management in RACF is based on the definition of users, groups, and access profiles. These mechanisms allow detailed security policies to be established, determining the permissions associated with each resource and facilitating efficient and consistent access management throughout the organization.
In addition to controlling access to resources, RACF provides advanced auditing and traceability capabilities. It records events related to access attempts, configuration changes, and user activities, enabling organizations to meet regulatory requirements, conduct security investigations, and detect unauthorized behavior.
RACF integrates natively with the z/OS operating system and with numerous IBM and third-party products, making it the de facto standard for security management in mainframe environments. Its robustness, scalability, and reliability have made it widely used in highly regulated sectors such as banking, insurance, government, telecommunications, and large corporations.
Today, RACF continues to evolve to meet modern security requirements, incorporating capabilities related to identity management, multifactor authentication, encryption, and regulatory compliance, while maintaining compatibility with legacy applications and systems.
languages.examples:
ADDUSER CARLOS DFLTGRP(USERS) PASSWORD(PASS123)
PERMIT 'APP.DATA' CLASS(DATASET) ID(CARLOS) ACCESS(READ)

languages.name: TSO
languages.shortDescription: Time Sharing Option. Interactive environment for executing commands and scripts in z/OS.
languages.longDescription:
Mainframes emerged during the 1960s and 1970s as batch-oriented machines that primarily operated using punched cards. The need for real-time interaction led to the development of time-sharing environments.
TSO (Time Sharing Option) was introduced to provide users with an interactive environment on mainframes, allowing them to execute commands and edit data directly. Initially introduced as an option in OS/360 systems, it became an essential part of the environment as systems evolved toward MVS and z/OS. Over time, its capabilities were extended into TSO/E (Time Sharing Option/Extensions), incorporating improvements in command execution, support for scripting languages such as REXX, and greater flexibility for editing and executing concurrent tasks.
TSO changed the traditional paradigm by allowing each user to have their own isolated environment, making it possible to work simultaneously without interference between processes and improving interactivity and multitasking.
The combination and integration of TSO with ISPF created a powerful environment for editing, developing, and managing datasets, where users can execute batch tasks and then switch to interactive mode for more detailed editing.
With TSO/E, advanced capabilities were added, including the ability to include commands in REXX scripts, which facilitated task automation, troubleshooting, and the integration of complex processes into the mainframe project lifecycle.
In summary, the evolution of mainframe editors reflects the need to move from rudimentary batch systems to highly interactive and productive environments. TSO and its evolution through TSO/E, together with ISPF, now provide a robust platform that not only facilitates data editing and management but also enables the automation and optimization of critical tasks in demanding environments.
languages.examples:
ALLOC DA('USER.TEST') F(TEST) SHR
LISTCAT LEVEL(USER)
FREE F(TEST)

languages.name: ISPF
languages.shortDescription: Interactive interface for editing, navigation, and development tools in z/OS.
languages.longDescription:
Although TSO initially provided a command-line interface for editing and managing files, users needed more interactive and visual tools to work efficiently.
ISPF (Interactive System Productivity Facility) emerged to fill this gap. This environment, integrated with TSO, provided a more user-friendly and robust editor, offering:
Full-screen editing with menus and interactive help.
Intuitive navigation through incremental line numbering, typically in increments of 10, making it easier to insert new lines without manually renumbering the existing ones.
Line editing commands, such as copy, insert, and delete, directly associated with line numbers, which accelerated the process of modifying code and documentation.
Automation and Scripting: TSO/E supports the use of REXX and CLIST for automating editing processes, streamlining repetitive tasks such as performing bulk modifications across a dataset.
Over the years, mainframes have also incorporated enhancements that enable the integration of modern features, such as Unix environments through UNIX System Services on z/OS. This has facilitated convergence between traditional mainframe editing techniques and modern tools, providing a more flexible experience adapted to contemporary requirements.
languages.examples:
A typical ISPF panel:
)BODY
%MENU
Select an option:
1 - Process
2 - Exit

languages.name: Java
languages.shortDescription: Object-oriented programming language widely used in enterprise applications and mainframe environments with z/OS.
languages.longDescription:
Java is a high-level, object-oriented programming language that can also be used in mainframe environments, particularly on IBM z/OS systems. Its main advantage in this environment is that it allows new applications and services to be developed that can work alongside traditional mainframe applications, such as those developed in COBOL.
Java uses the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which allows programs to run on different systems as long as a compatible JVM is available. On a mainframe, Java can run on z/OS and take advantage of the system's resources and processing capacity. This makes it possible to combine Java capabilities with the security, stability, and processing power of mainframes.
As in other environments, Java uses variables, conditions, loops, methods, classes, and objects. Its programming model is primarily object-oriented, using concepts such as encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism. Java programs are compiled into bytecode, which is subsequently executed by the JVM.
An important characteristic of Java on the mainframe is its ability to integrate with other systems and technologies. It can work with databases such as DB2, transaction systems such as CICS, and messaging systems such as MQ. It can also communicate with existing applications developed in languages such as COBOL, enabling legacy systems to be modernized without having to replace them completely.
Java can be used on the mainframe to develop enterprise applications, services, data-processing processes, and components that communicate with existing applications. This allows an organization to maintain its traditional systems while incorporating more modern technologies.
Java on the mainframe retains the fundamental characteristics of the Java language, but it is particularly valuable because of its ability to integrate with the mainframe ecosystem. Its compatibility with technologies such as z/OS, CICS, DB2, and MQ, together with its ability to work with existing applications, makes it a useful tool for developing and modernizing enterprise systems.

languages.name: z/OS UNIX
languages.shortDescription: UNIX environment integrated into z/OS that provides POSIX services and tools for running applications and scripts.
languages.longDescription:
UNIX on the mainframe primarily refers to z/OS UNIX System Services (USS), a UNIX environment integrated into the IBM z/OS operating system. Its purpose is to provide users and developers with a UNIX-compatible environment within the mainframe, allowing applications, commands, and UNIX-style scripts to run while retaining the traditional capabilities of the z/OS system.
USS provides a hierarchical file system similar to those used by other UNIX systems. Files and directories are organized using paths and permissions that control access to information. Users can use commands to create, copy, move, delete, and inspect files and directories. Common commands include ls, cd, cp, mv, and rm.
One of the main characteristics of USS is the use of a shell, which allows commands and scripts to be executed. Through the shell, tasks can be automated, programs can be executed, and files can be managed. It is also possible to use tools and applications originally developed for UNIX environments, adapting them to z/OS when necessary.
USS is integrated with the rest of the z/OS environment, allowing it to work alongside traditional mainframe applications. This makes it possible to combine programs developed in languages such as COBOL, C, or PL/I with applications and processes running in the UNIX environment. In this way, organizations can leverage existing systems while adding new technologies without replacing the entire infrastructure.
Another important characteristic is its ability to work with mainframe data and services. Applications running in USS can communicate with systems such as DB2 and CICS, as well as use other services available in z/OS. They can also exchange information with external applications through networks and different communication protocols.
USS is particularly useful for developing and running modern applications within the mainframe. It can be used to run programs written in languages such as Java, Python, or C/C++, as well as scripts and other tools. This facilitates integration between traditional mainframe applications and technologies currently in use.
Security is another fundamental aspect. USS uses z/OS security mechanisms, such as RACF, to control users and their access permissions. This makes it possible to protect system files, programs, and resources while maintaining a high level of security, which is especially important in sectors such as banking, insurance, and large enterprises.
z/OS UNIX System Services is the UNIX environment integrated into the IBM z/OS mainframe. It provides UNIX tools, commands, file systems, and capabilities while allowing applications and resources to work alongside traditional mainframe systems. This integration makes USS an important component for system modernization and enables current technologies to be incorporated while preserving the stability, security, and processing capabilities characteristic of mainframes.
languages.examples:
cd /u/user01
ls -la
cat archivo.txt
export APP_HOME=/u/user01/app

languages.name: C
languages.shortDescription: General-purpose programming language used on z/OS for systems, utilities, and high-performance applications.
languages.longDescription:
C is a general-purpose programming language created in the early 1970s by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs. Its development was closely related to the UNIX operating system, as C was used to develop a large part of the system. Over the years, C became one of the most important programming languages and has influenced many modern languages.
One of the main characteristics of C is that it is relatively close to the computer's internal operation. It allows direct interaction with elements such as memory, addresses, and pointers. At the same time, it provides programming structures such as variables, functions, conditions, and loops that facilitate the creation of organized programs.
C is known for being fast, efficient, and flexible. Programs written in C are typically compiled directly into code that the processor can execute, providing good performance. C also allows computer resources to be used relatively directly, which is particularly important when memory and processing capacity must be fully utilized.
Another important characteristic is that C is portable. This means that a C program can be adapted to run on different operating systems and types of computers with some modifications. For this reason, C has been widely used in systems where performance and resource control are important.
C is used in many areas of computing. For example, it is used to develop operating systems, device drivers, embedded systems, low-level programs, and applications requiring high performance. It has also been used to develop software related to networking, databases, and system utilities.
Learning C can also help developers better understand how computers work. Concepts such as pointers, dynamic memory, data structures, and compilation allow programmers to understand aspects that other languages may hide.
C has also had a major influence on other languages. C++, C#, Java, and many other languages share concepts or features related to C. For this reason, learning C can provide a good foundation for subsequently studying other programming languages.
C is a fundamental language in the history of computing. Despite being several decades old, it continues to be used because of its speed, efficiency, and ability to work directly with computer resources. Its importance lies not only in the programs it enables developers to build, but also in the influence it has had on numerous subsequent languages and technologies.

languages.name: C++
languages.shortDescription: Compiled programming language used for high-performance applications and enterprise components on z/OS.
languages.longDescription:
C++ is a general-purpose programming language derived from C. It is characterized by being fast and efficient and can be used to create anything from simple programs to complex applications. It is a compiled language, meaning that the source code written by the programmer is transformed by a compiler into a program that the computer can execute.
A C++ program consists of instructions that are normally executed from the main function, called main(). The cout object is used to display information, while cin is used to receive keyboard input. Variables are used to store data during program execution. Common basic types include int for integer numbers, double for decimal numbers, char for characters, and bool for true or false values. The string type is also used to store text.
C++ provides different operators for performing operations. Arithmetic operators allow addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and remainder calculations. Comparison operators allow two values to be compared for equality, inequality, or relative magnitude. Logical operators allow multiple conditions to be combined.
Conditional structures such as if, else if, and else are used to make decisions. They allow different instructions to be executed depending on whether a particular condition is met. The switch statement can also be used to select one option from several possibilities.
Loops are used to repeat instructions. The for loop is commonly used when the number of repetitions is known, while while is used when repetition should continue as long as a condition remains true. do while is similar to while but guarantees that the instructions are executed at least once.
Functions allow a program to be divided into smaller, reusable parts. A function can receive data through parameters and return a result using return. This facilitates program organization, understanding, and maintenance.
C++ also supports arrays and vectors, which are used to store multiple related values. In addition, it includes pointers, which allow direct work with memory addresses, and references, which provide an alternative name for a variable.
One of the most important characteristics of C++ is object-oriented programming. This programming model uses classes and objects. A class acts as a template defining the data and behavior that its objects will have. The data members are known as attributes, while the functions associated with a class are known as methods. The main concepts of object-oriented programming include encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.
C++ is a powerful and efficient language that supports variables, operations, conditions, loops, functions, and objects. Its ability to control many aspects of computer operation makes it suitable for applications, video games, operating systems, and other software where performance is important.

languages.name: Python
languages.shortDescription: High-level language used in z/OS UNIX for automation, scripting, integration, and tool development.
languages.longDescription:
Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language. It was created by Guido van Rossum and is characterized by a simple and easy-to-understand syntax. Thanks to these characteristics, Python is one of the most widely used languages both for learning programming and for professional application development.
Python allows programs to be created using instructions that are executed sequentially. Variables are used to store information, and their type does not need to be explicitly declared in advance. Common data types include int for integer numbers, float for decimal numbers, str for text, and bool for true or false values. It also provides structures such as lists, tuples, and dictionaries for storing multiple values.
The print() function is primarily used to display information, while input() allows data entered by the user to be received. Python provides arithmetic operators for calculations, comparison operators for comparing values, and logical operators for combining different conditions.
Conditional structures allow decisions to be made within a program. The main constructs are if, elif, and else, which allow different instructions to be executed depending on whether certain conditions are met. Loops, on the other hand, allow instructions to be repeated. The for loop is normally used to iterate over elements or repeat an action a specified number of times, while while repeats instructions as long as a condition remains true.
Functions allow a program to be divided into smaller, reusable parts. They are defined using def and can receive parameters and return a result using return. This helps organize code and avoids repeating the same instructions multiple times.
Python also supports modules and libraries containing pre-built functions and tools that can be incorporated into programs. Well-known libraries include NumPy for numerical calculations, Pandas for working with data, and Matplotlib for creating charts. This extensive library ecosystem allows Python to be used across many different fields.
One of Python's main advantages is its versatility. It is used in web development, task automation, data analysis, artificial intelligence, machine learning, scientific computing, and script development, among many other areas. It is also a cross-platform language, allowing it to be used on different operating systems.
Python is a simple, flexible, and powerful language characterized by clear syntax and a large ecosystem of available tools. Its ease of learning and wide range of applications have made it one of the most important and widely used programming languages today.

languages.name: SQL
languages.shortDescription: Query and data manipulation language primarily used with DB2 in mainframe environments.
languages.longDescription:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is a language primarily used to create, query, and manage relational databases. Unlike languages such as C++ or Fortran, SQL is specifically designed to work with information stored in tables. It is widely used in applications and enterprise systems to store, organize, query, and modify large amounts of data.
A relational database organizes information into tables consisting of rows and columns. Each column represents a type of data, such as a name, age, or date, while each row contains the data corresponding to a record. Tables can be related to one another through common fields, allowing information to be organized efficiently and reducing data duplication.
SQL supports different operations on a database. The SELECT statement is used to query and retrieve information. INSERT adds new records, UPDATE modifies existing information, and DELETE removes records. These statements are fundamental for working with stored data.
Conditions can also be used to retrieve only the information of interest. The WHERE clause allows filters to be specified in a query. ORDER BY sorts the results, while GROUP BY groups records to perform operations on them. SQL also provides functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, and MIN for performing calculations on data.
Another important characteristic of SQL is the ability to create and modify the structure of databases. Statements such as CREATE, ALTER, and DROP can be used to create, modify, or delete tables and other database objects. Constraints can also be defined to ensure that stored data is valid and consistent.
Databases typically use primary keys to uniquely identify each record. They can also use foreign keys to establish relationships between tables. These relationships make it possible to query information from multiple tables using operations known as JOINs.
SQL is used by numerous database management systems, including MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server, and SQLite. Although there are differences between them, they all use SQL as the foundation for working with data.
SQL is a fundamental language for managing relational databases. It allows information to be stored, queried, modified, and deleted, as well as enabling different tables to be related and calculations to be performed on data. Its simplicity and usefulness have made it an essential technology in web applications, enterprise systems, and virtually any program that needs to store and manage information.

languages.name: Bash
languages.shortDescription: Shell and scripting language used in UNIX environments, including z/OS UNIX, for task automation.
languages.longDescription:
Bash is a command interpreter or shell primarily used on Unix-based operating systems, especially Linux. Its name stands for Bourne Again SHell, a play on the Bourne Shell, one of the first major Unix command interpreters.
Bash allows users to communicate with the operating system through commands entered in a terminal. Instead of relying exclusively on graphical interfaces with windows and buttons, users can enter instructions to execute programs, manage files, configure the system, and automate tasks.
To understand the origin of Bash, it is necessary to go back to Unix, an operating system developed in the 1970s at Bell Labs. Unix introduced a philosophy in which many tasks could be performed using small programs and commands that could be combined with one another.
One of the first important command interpreters was the Bourne Shell (sh), developed by Stephen Bourne in the 1970s. Over time, different shells appeared and added new features.
In the late 1980s, Brian Fox developed Bash for the GNU project, initiated by Richard Stallman. Bash was designed as a free and compatible alternative to the Bourne Shell while incorporating additional features.
The first version of Bash appeared in 1989. It subsequently evolved and became one of the most widely used shells on Linux and other Unix systems.
Bash has many uses. One of the most important is system administration. An administrator can use Bash commands to create users, manage files, inspect processes, modify permissions, or control services. Although highly advanced graphical interfaces are now available, Bash remains important because it allows certain tasks to be performed quickly, precisely, and automatically.
For example, a system administrator may need to perform an operation on hundreds of files. Instead of modifying each file manually, they can write a small script that performs the task automatically.
Bash is also widely used in programming and DevOps, where processes such as program compilation, deployments, backups, and server administration need to be automated.
languages.examples:
#!/bin/bash
for f in /u/user01/data/*.txt; do
  echo "Processing $f"
done

languages.name: Natural
languages.shortDescription: Fourth-generation programming language historically used in enterprise applications and mainframe systems.
languages.longDescription:
Natural is a fourth-generation programming language developed by Software AG. It was primarily designed to facilitate the development of enterprise applications and the access and processing of large amounts of data. Its syntax is relatively simple and allows programs to be created using less code than more traditional programming languages.
Natural is particularly used in enterprise systems and applications that need to work with databases. One of its main characteristics is its integration with Adabas, a database management system also developed by Software AG. This integration allows Natural to query, modify, insert, and delete information in a simple and efficient manner.
Natural programs consist of instructions that specify the operations to be performed by the computer. The language allows variables to be used to store information such as numbers, characters, or dates. It also provides instructions for displaying information and receiving user input.
Natural supports conditional structures for making decisions. Through instructions such as IF and ELSE, a program can perform different actions depending on whether a particular condition is met. It also provides repetition structures that allow a set of instructions to be executed multiple times, which is especially useful when processing large amounts of data.
Another important characteristic of Natural is its use of modules and subprograms, which allow an application to be divided into different parts. This facilitates code organization, reuse, and maintenance. Programs can perform calculations, process information, and communicate with databases to retrieve or modify the required data.
Natural is particularly focused on enterprise information processing. For this reason, it has been used for many years in sectors such as banking, insurance, government, and large enterprises. Although it is an older language compared with many current programming languages, it continues to be used in numerous enterprise systems because of the large number of existing applications developed with Natural.
Natural is a programming language primarily focused on enterprise application development and data processing. Its simple syntax, ease of database integration, and ability to process large volumes of information have made it a long-standing technology in the IT systems of large organizations.
languages.examples:
DEFINE DATA LOCAL
1 #NOMBRE (A30)
END-DEFINE
INPUT #NOMBRE
WRITE #NOMBRE
END

languages.name: Fortran
languages.shortDescription: Programming language used primarily for scientific computing, numerical computation, and engineering applications.
languages.longDescription:
Fortran is a programming language originally created for scientific and mathematical calculations. Its name comes from “FORmula TRANslator” and it was developed in the 1950s. It is one of the oldest programming languages still in use, particularly in fields such as engineering, physics, meteorology, and scientific research, where large numbers of calculations need to be performed quickly and efficiently.
A Fortran program consists of instructions that tell the computer which operations to perform. Modern programs typically begin with the program keyword and end with end program. Variables are used to store data and must have a defined type. Common types include integer for whole numbers, real for decimal numbers, character for text, and logical for true or false values. Variables are usually declared at the beginning of the program.
The print statement is primarily used to display information, while read allows data to be entered through the keyboard. Fortran also supports mathematical operations using operators such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. In addition, it provides built-in mathematical functions for more complex operations.
Conditional structures such as if, else if, and else are used to make decisions. They allow different instructions to be executed depending on whether a condition is met. The select case construct can also be used to choose between different options.
Fortran provides repetition structures known as loops. The do loop allows a set of instructions to be repeated a specified number of times or while a condition is met. Loops are particularly important in Fortran because they enable repetitive calculations to be performed efficiently.
Functions and subroutines allow a program to be divided into different parts. A function performs an operation and returns a result, while a subroutine can perform a series of operations without necessarily returning a single value directly. Using these constructs facilitates code organization and reuse.
One of Fortran's most important characteristics is its ability to work with arrays, which allow large amounts of data to be stored in one or more dimensions. This is particularly useful in scientific computing, for example when representing matrices, vectors, or data obtained from simulations.
Fortran has evolved over time, and modern versions include features such as modular programming, user-defined data types, and object-oriented programming. Despite its age, it remains in use because of its efficiency and the large amount of scientific software developed with it.
Fortran is a language specifically designed for numerical and scientific computing. It stands out for its efficiency, its ability to work with large amounts of data, and its support for complex mathematical operations. For these reasons, it remains important in scientific and engineering fields.
languages.examples:
PROGRAM HELLO
      PRINT *, "HELLO MAINFRAME"
      END
